item.title: The Real Magic of Journaling Happens off the Page
item.description:
Self-Help

The Real Magic of Journaling Happens off the Page

Journal your way to becoming a person for whom breakthroughs are possible.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • Like exercise, journaling's benefits often become apparent gradually, through consistent practice.
  • Pairing journaling with meditation helped me capture fleeting thoughts.
  • One size does not fit all when it comes to journaling.

I’ve been a journal skeptic for most of my life. But recently, I realized I’d been looking at the thing all wrong. I mistakenly believed I was not journaling material. That my life was too mundane, too ordinary, and maybe—dare I say—too private to put down on paper, where my children could one day read my innermost thoughts.

I think I was trying to make the practice into a memoir—like the epic Diary of Samuel Pepys. Like so many things, journaling is what you make it.

Three things I believe to be true about journaling

  • One size does not fit all.
  • There is no right way to journal.
  • The benefits reveal themselves almost imperceptibly over a long, long time.

For years, people have given me blank, empty journals. Why? I guess because I’m a writer, and sometimes a wannabe writer who doesn’t write enough; therefore, a journal can serve as a blank slate onto which one ideates, reflects, and plans.

Those gifted blank journals never inspired me to write. Not a single word. Rather, they taunted me from a nightstand table or a shelf in my room. Of course, I said, “Thank you so much,” every time a well-meaning friend gave me one of those lovely blank books. Some I regifted. Others I donated along with other unwanted books.

In truth, I just didn’t know how to start. Like a pair of dumbbells propped against a door, I didn’t know how to begin. (Maybe I could make those blank journals into a doorstop?)

I started watching videos about journaling. Ryder Carroll, creator of the Bullet Journal method, inspired me to pick up a blank journal with no lines but rather a grid of light gray dots.

Look at the plethora of videos about "BuJo," and you will quickly feel as embarrassed as I did when seeing the beautiful spreads that influencers have created on those lovely blank pages. They connected the dots to make grids, calendars, and habit trackers. Some wrote in beautiful scripts, others employed stamps, and still others colored the pages with markers and watercolors. They transformed those double-page spreads into works of art.

My journal attempts only taunted me with the ugly shapes of my own handwritten lines.

One woman showed me how to make pockets, Dutch doors, and hinges.

Researchers, too, have taken up the "BuJo" mantle. “Particularly noteworthy is how Bullet Journals function as a self-regulation tool, encouraging users to design notebook layouts and content based on their current psychological needs” (Almeida da Silva et al., 2025).

I tried. I really did try. I carefully drew my own four-month calendar and added in important dates as reminders of what was coming up in the next season. But appointment calendars lose their effect when you don’t remember to look at them. My journal rested on my nightstand. Reminders didn’t remind me. Dates slipped away.

Journal in the morning to plan your day. Journal at night to reflect on your day. Carry a pocket-sized Field Notes journal to write down your thoughts throughout the day.

I kept a pocket journal in my purse. It ended up being a nice, safe place to store receipts that were often useful for bookkeeping, but not for mind-expanding thoughts.

Then something miraculous happened. I tried meditating on my lack of journaling skills. I had followed the practice of sitting quietly for 20 minutes each morning contemplating. But meditation is another practice I have failed at. My ADHD brain constantly ping-pongs from one idea to another.

Some great ideas evaporated before my session ended because I simply forgot the thought, even when, at the same time, I was thinking, "Oh, I’ll remember that for sure."

Finally, I thought, "What if I set my open journal on my lap while I meditated?" No intention, just an invitation to capture those fleeting thoughts before they disappear.

Productive Meditation

Suddenly, meditating became productive in a positive way, and journaling felt useful.

Maybe it was the dimness of my morning bedroom. Maybe it was the informality of my writing. It didn’t matter that my handwriting was bad. It just felt useful to have this depository for my ideas.

After the 20 minutes, and after breakfast and coffee, I sometimes reread the morning’s notes and organize and clarify those random ideas. I highlight the best ones, making them easier to find later. Ten minutes of this focused analysis yielded ideas for articles, YouTube video scripts, and projects. I could sort out the steps to begin, tackle, and finish long-standing "someday maybe" projects.

I captured those ideas neatly within the covers of my journals.

Journaling has helped me tackle "ghost" projects simply because I can see my notes and revisit them. I can add to the notes. I can copy them over. I can even tear out pages.

In the end, I realized that journaling is a lot like going to the gym. You don’t see the benefits at first. But after a while, you notice that you can lift that heavy grocery bag or move that overstuffed chair without complaint. Your muscles are stronger. Your endurance has increased. Your lung capacity has improved.

Maybe the real magic of journaling is not what happens on the page. Maybe it’s what becomes possible off the page.

item.title: I Know You Are, But What Am I?
item.description:
Bullying

I Know You Are, But What Am I?

Name-calling doesn’t just hurt its target. It tells everyone what's acceptable.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • Name-calling that targets identity is linked to shame.
  • Insults aimed at women's bodies reinforce self-objectification.
  • Public insults signal to onlookers what is acceptable.

On October 10, comedian Shane Gillis hosted Saturday Night Live and used his monologue to say that women at the gym now dress like “whores.” The backlash was immediate. Actor and writer Dan Levy posted on Instagram, saying that short shorts don’t make women whores; they make the men calling them that misogynists.

Gillis’ comment couldn’t have come at a worse time. The country was in a heated argument over the Cornell case, a civil lawsuit in which a former student (Jane Doe) alleges that seven men drugged and raped her at a fraternity party. Underneath the debate sits an old question: whether a woman’s appearance and choices make her responsible for what happens to her. Gillis’ joke hit right at the heart of it.

Same insult, different stage

Last November, aboard Air Force One, Bloomberg’s Catherine Lucey asked President Trump about an Epstein email. He pointed at her and said, “Quiet, piggy.” The White House didn’t apologize. Instead, it accused the reporter of unprofessional behavior. This wasn’t the first time Trump used that word. Former Miss Universe Alicia Machado has said Trump called her “Miss Piggy.”

Name-calling isn’t exclusive to men. Discussing the Cornell case, podcaster Megyn Kelly described the woman at the center as “not the most attractive gal.” When singer Olivia Rodrigo voiced her support for Jane Doe, Kelly called her a “know-nothing moron” and told her to shut up and stick to singing.

Name-calling aimed at a woman’s body can be especially harmful. Objectification theory holds that when women are repeatedly reduced to how they look, many begin to watch themselves through that lens, a habit linked to shame, anxiety, and depression (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997).

"Sticks and stones" was always a lie

I was taught that names can never hurt me. The research says otherwise. In a 2006 study of 554 young adults, psychiatrist Martin Teicher at Harvard’s McLean Hospital found that childhood exposure to parental verbal aggression had moderate to large effects on depression, anxiety, and dissociation (Teicher et al., 2006). A follow-up found that verbal abuse from peers was tied to higher psychiatric symptoms and measurable differences in the brain’s white matter (Teicher et al., 2010).

What makes a name hurt depends on what it targets. Psychologists distinguish between criticizing behavior and judging the self. Research on shame and guilt shows that feeling bad about something you did tends to motivate repair, whereas feeling bad about who you are is more closely linked to depression, anxiety, and defensive anger (Tangney & Dearing, 2002).

Here are two examples:

  • “What you did was selfish” criticizes behavior.
  • “You’re selfish” converts criticism into a verdict on who you are.

Context matters too

Teasing and nicknames can be affectionate or cruel depending on the relationship and the intent behind them (Keltner et al., 2001). A name does the most damage when it’s unwanted and targets something central to identity.

I learned this in sixth grade. A classmate started calling me Smelly Spinelli. It caught on, and eventually I was just Smelly. It didn’t do much damage, because I never thought of myself as someone particularly malodorous. The name described a smell I didn’t have.

What cut deep was being called queer. That name didn’t describe something I did. It named something about who I was and turned it into an indictment. Every time a classmate called me queer, I became smaller and smaller. Because I believed that if I became small enough, the word couldn’t hurt me.

Who says it matters

Social psychologist Thomas Ford calls this prejudiced norm theory. Many people with prejudiced views tend to keep them quiet because they fear social disapproval. Disparaging humor lowers that fear. The joke frame signals to everyone listening: It’s OK. Relax. I’m only kidding.

The kids who called me queer didn’t create the prejudice in that classroom. They provided everyone else with permission.

Ford’s work suggests comedians deserve the scrutiny they get, because the joke frame is uniquely disarming. But humor isn’t the only way to grant permission. Status does it too. After the 2016 election, Americans judged it more acceptable to express prejudice toward groups Trump had targeted (Crandall et al., 2018). When a president or a podcaster uses a slur, the message is clear: “People like me say this all the time, and nothing happens.”

I know you are, but what am I?

Shane Gillis should be held accountable for what he said, and so should the producers who aired it. But we can’t hold a comedian accountable for degrading women without seeing the bigger picture. We live in a culture where name-calling has become the grown-up version of the playground comeback. It flows from the podium, the podcast, and the press gaggle, and each insult makes the next one easier.

Words do real harm to the people they target and quietly shift what the rest of us accept. So, by all means, criticize comedians. Then turn the same scrutiny upward, toward the people whose words carry far more weight.

item.title: Why Is It Harder for Men to Be Vulnerable With Each Other?
item.description:
Friends

Why Is It Harder for Men to Be Vulnerable With Each Other?

"The North" explores male loneliness, friendship, and vulnerability.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • "The North" looks at how masculine expectations and changing lives can complicate men's friendships.
  • Understanding male friendship means examining how men experience connection, vulnerability, and change.
  • Old friendships change with life’s demands; accepting this can allow relationships to evolve.
Source: "The North"/Tuesday Studio

I had the pleasure of speaking with filmmaker Bart Schrijver and actors Bart Harder and Carles Pulido about their beautiful new film, The North.

With breathtaking cinematography set against the Scottish Highlands, The North follows two former best friends, Chris (Bart Harder) and Lluis (Carles Pulido), who reunite to hike 330 miles together after not seeing one another for 10 years. Hoping to reconnect, they find their conversations interrupted, their frustrations hard to describe, and the intimacy they once shared more challenging to recover than they thought.

Harder and Pulido first met through the project, and the warmth between them was apparent even over Zoom. “We immediately became friends… in real life,” Pulido said. Harder agreed: “The friendship thing was kind of natural.”

As the relationship between their characters became more strained, however, Pulido began intentionally distancing himself from Harder during filming, sometimes walking alone for hours. During our interview, it occurred to him that he had never actually asked Harder what that was like for him, so he asked him right then. Harder explained that because they had developed “such a beautiful start, and a real friendship,” he understood when Pulido needed space. “It was totally fine,” he laughed. It was one of the sweetest moments of the interview, demonstrating that their bond had become secure enough to withstand the space the filming process required without experiencing it as a threat to their actual friendship.

Schrijver explained that the idea for the film came from his own experience hiking in New Zealand with a friend. They spent months together, even sharing a tent. Years later, skimming through his travel diary, he noticed that although they were physically together the whole time, they weren’t always emotionally connected.

As a psychotherapist who works with many men navigating relationships, identity, and intimacy, I was drawn to the film’s honest portrayal of male friendship. We are having more and more conversations about male loneliness, often accompanied by the suggestion that men just need to talk more about their feelings. However, these discussions are incomplete without looking at how men experience closeness, or why being emotionally vulnerable with another man can feel threatening.

Throughout my clinical career, I have witnessed how people approach friendship differently. While women frequently describe meeting specifically “to talk,” men often connect through shared activities, side by side. They play sports, go hiking, watch games, or grab a drink.

“I think it has to do with how men treat vulnerability,” Pulido said. He described how men may feel the need to protect themselves from a world that can feel hostile and rejecting of open displays of emotion.

“I guess men learn, the hard way or not, to create a shield around us,” Pulido reflected.

When two people sit across from each other with the explicit expectation of emotional disclosure, the intensity of being observed can heighten self-consciousness. In side-by-side connection, eye contact becomes optional, silence feels less conspicuous, and conversation can unfold without pressure.

“No one, at least in my experience, no one… showed me how, or taught me how to bring my guard down,” Pulido said.

He explained that among male friends it can feel more comfortable to invite someone to do an activity together. “But unconsciously, we are… meeting to talk.”

Harder described hiking with his own group of male friends, who make an effort to check in, with most conversations evolving naturally as they walk side by side.

“At a certain point you walk with this guy and say, ‘Hey, how are you really doing?’”

Vulnerability as a Threat to Masculinity

Men may be encouraged to be emotionally available while simultaneously receiving the message that vulnerability makes them weak.

I've encountered male survivors who feel ashamed of having experienced trauma because they believe they should have fought back. Others fear that expressing sadness, rejection, or emotional dependency will make them appear less masculine. Some have described being mocked by male friends for admitting heartbreak or disclosing an assault, reinforcing the very silence that keeps them isolated.

“I think the misunderstanding sometimes is that men don't have those emotions or have less,” Schrijver said.

“There's a lot of anger, because that's an emotion that men are allowed to have,” Schrijver said.

When Old Friendships Change

For Schrijver, part of making The North involved accepting that some friendships cannot return to what they once were. Careers develop, romantic relationships deepen, families begin, and priorities change. Differences that mattered little in youth can become more consequential with age.

Chris has followed a relatively conventional path, with a demanding career, a romantic relationship, and responsibilities that repeatedly intrude on the trip. Lluis, meanwhile, is questioning his direction and searching for fulfillment. Schrijver described the men as experiencing different economic and social realities while having remarkably similar internal struggles. Both are trapped, in different ways, by expectations they have imposed upon themselves.

“Even though you haven't seen or talked to each other for that long, you still call each other best friend,” Schrijver said. “The moment that you're OK with things not being the way they used to be, then there's new space for the relationship to evolve into something else.”

Harder reflected on how painful it can be to recognize that a friendship has changed, since, unlike romantic relationships, friendships rarely come with formal endings.

In therapy, I often see people struggling to reconcile who someone used to be with who they have become. We expect old friends to understand us and show up for us, and we can feel betrayed when they no longer do. Reconnecting can require relinquishing the friendship we remember and becoming curious about each other again. In The North, Chris and Lluis are learning whether they can make room for the people they have become.

Vulnerability Is More Than Talking About Feelings

Schrijver deliberately allows moments of silence to linger rather than rescuing the audience from the discomfort. Pulido described the silence as giving the audience “the time to enter the experience themselves.”

Vulnerability requires courage from the person sharing and receptivity from the person listening. Being emotionally vulnerable means allowing ourselves to be witnessed in our suffering, while both people tolerate the discomfort without rushing to fix it.

Schrijver also described how restricting our emotional range can leave life feeling flat. “If you never cry, then you take out a bit of the low part, then you also take a bit out of the top part.”

One of the film’s most moving scenes captures a breakthrough between the two friends and the reality that true intimacy does not depend on how eloquently someone can describe their internal experience. In fact, often the very opposite is true. I won't spoil it, because you should see it for yourself, but it involves two friends struggling to find their way back toward each other.

I highly recommend seeing The North, this visually magnificent, emotionally raw, extraordinary movie, in theaters. Perhaps afterward, invite a friend for a walk. You never know where the conversation could take you.

item.title: Why Horror Belongs in the Classroom
item.description:
Education

Why Horror Belongs in the Classroom

A good scare engages the mind, opens important topics, and may build resilience.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • Horror can be an excellent teaching tool.
  • Students can explore fear by comparing their experiences with physiological measurements.
  • A jump scare raised average heart rate by 13 bpm; scenes of dread left it flat but stilled the room.
  • A supernatural horror story can spark discussions of real issues like consent, coercion, and bodily autonomy.
A group of student research assistants at Dystopia Haunted House, being instructed by Recreational Fear Lab co-director Marc Andersen.
Source: Mathias Clasen

Why would I, as a university lecturer, want to scare the daylights out of my students?

I can think of two good reasons. First, horror can be an excellent Trojan horse of learning. Stories of vampires, zombies, and horrors from beyond the grave engage attention while inviting psychological and aesthetic analysis. Second, voluntary encounters with manageable fear may help people practice regulating difficult emotions. That's part of the appeal of recreational fear.

A Course in Recreational Fear

For years, I have been teaching an undergraduate elective course called Recreational Fear: Scientific, Historical, and Aesthetic Perspectives. The course introduces students to the field’s foundations, methods, and latest findings, and prepares them to write a bachelor’s project at the intersection of English Studies and recreational fear. They can also join our Recreational Fear Lab as research assistants during field studies at Dystopia Haunted House. It’s a win-win: Students get experience with empirical data collection, and we get valuable help.

The course moves from basic research on fear and anxiety to recreational fear and its potential therapeutic effects, with horror as the main case study. I have the students read Stephen King’s Pet Sematary—possibly the scariest book in existence, but also an incredibly psychologically rich novel (Clasen, 2020)—as well as watch a scary movie and play some horror video games.

A fireside horror story, told by Danish horror writer Michael Kamp.
Source: Mathias Clasen

Paleo Horror by the Bonfire

For the fall 2026 edition of the course, I organized a field trip to the darkest heart of Jutland. The destination was a remote woodland campsite, where I had hired one of Denmark's scariest horror writers, Michael Kamp, to entertain my students with a frightening tale. We had a bonfire going and pizza waiting. After eating, the students gathered around the fire and spent 30 minutes utterly rapt in Kamp's story.

The point was to let students experience horror entertainment the way our ancestors experienced it for thousands of years—in a group, with a blazing fire in front of them and oppressive darkness at their backs, imaginations running at top capacity. No screens, no distractions, just story. It was an experience in "paleo horror," as my boss put it, and an enormous success. It also provided material for discussions of horror's deep history, its social dimensions, and the differences between oral, written, and audiovisual storytelling.

Still from "Obsession" (2026), a genuinely scary horror movie with exquisite Trojan horse potential.
Source: NBCUniversal / Used with permission

Movie Night, With Sensors

The following week was movie week, with a focus on the 2026 movie Obsession. Bear, a twentysomething with an unrequited crush on his friend Nikki, uses dark magic to make her love him more than anything in the world. That quickly turns very dark: Nikki will stop at nothing to pursue her unnatural obsession.

The dozen or so students who attended the screening wore heart-rate monitors and completed questionnaires about their expected and actual fear and enjoyment. Two days later, we met to look at the physiological results and discuss the movie.

The students found the film somewhat less frightening than expected. In other research, we have found that some people, particularly those less comfortable with uncertainty, overestimate how negatively they will feel during a horror experience (FitzGibbon et al., 2025). Still, these students engaged enthusiastically with the film’s most powerful scenes and themes. One scene in particular—which involves a car window and an extremely well-orchestrated jump scare—really got their hearts racing. Within seconds, the class average rose by 13 beats per minute, the largest rise of the film. Individual students' heart rates jumped by between 9 and 51 beats per minute.

Heart rates around the car-window scare in "Obsession." Each gray line is one student; the red line is the class average.
Source: Mathias Clasen

When Dread Makes You Freeze

Intriguingly, other scenes we identified as deeply frightening barely registered in heart rates. When the possessed Nikki stands in the darkness in the corner of Bear's bedroom, for instance, the accelerometers built into the monitors suggest that students moved exceptionally little. That minute was one of the two with the least recorded movement in the whole film. The other was another quiet, dark scene with Nikki as the eerie threat.

Heart rate (top) and movement in the seats (bottom) across the whole film. The two minutes with the least recorded movement, marked in red, came during quiet scenes with Nikki as the threat. Heart rate barely changed in either. The dotted stretch around 1:25 marks two and a half minutes left out because of a disturbance in the room.
Source: Mathias Clasen

How can we make sense of these responses? The jump scare presents an imminent threat, and the body mobilizes—hence the racing hearts and the literal jump in the seats. A slow-burn, dread-inspiring scene may engage a different defensive response. An animal that spots a predator at a distance freezes: It goes still, its senses sharpen, and its heart tends to slow rather than speed up (Roelofs, 2017). That may be the difference between the two kinds of horror scenes: One, the jump scare, triggers an acute startle response; the other may evoke freezing-like vigilance.

The Trojan Horse at Work

Triangulating physiological measures and subjective impressions provided excellent material for classroom discussion—not just about the film, but about such larger academic issues as what different kinds of evidence can and cannot tell us. Physiological and behavioral measures may be objective in a way that self-report measures are not, but subjective reports can add richness and texture beyond what a heart rate monitor can capture. And the two did not always agree: How strongly a student’s heart reacted to the car-window scare said little about how much fear that student reported. The discussions also allowed us to connect cinematic analysis with psychological response, for instance, by analyzing particularly effective scenes to figure out how the filmmakers created suspense, dread, and horror.

And Obsession uses an unrealistic premise to address very real fears. My students felt that its themes were relevant to their own concerns: consent, bodily autonomy, the MeToo movement, and the incel phenomenon. Bear gets what he wants by overriding what Nikki wants, in a truly terrifying way. For some students, he came to embody the fear that a monster may hide inside someone who looks perfectly normal.

These excursions into horror—and into the science of horror—proved fun as well as instructive. That’s the Trojan horse at work: Students probably signed up expecting some entertaining material, but before they knew what hit them, they had tested their limits, peeked into the darkness, and learned something about fear, anxiety, and the power of supernatural horror to address real-world issues. They had not just felt fear; they had learned how to investigate it—and perhaps a little about how to cope with it, too.

My thanks to the students for their enthusiasm, curiosity, and thoughtful discussions, to Michael Kamp for the fireside story, and to Peter Mortensen for greenlighting the excursion.

item.title: Twin Identity: Growing Up and Growing Apart
item.description:
Understanding Twins

Twin Identity: Growing Up and Growing Apart

These strategies can enhance twin attachment and reduce unhappiness and anger.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • Separating from a twin and developing individuality is a gradual, challenging process.
  • Non-twins may struggle to understand twins’ unique communication and closeness.
  • Twins may feel guilt for not sharing, complicating the development of individuality.
Source: Halfpoint/iStock

My interest in twins is personal, professional, and profound. As far back as I can remember, curious strangers always asked my sister and me, “Are you twins?” when they saw us together. Often, being a twin generated a lot of entertainment, attention, comfort, and approval for both of us. Alongside the good times, however, were horrendous fights over who got more ice cream, or who was right and who was wrong. Whatever was happening, for better or worse, I was an identical twin.

And I still am an identical twin who has been asked over and over again by people who know both of us, "Which one are you?" This question still hurts, along with too much curiosity from strangers about my/our twinship.

Additionally, my long-standing interest in twin development is based on my own unique "twin superpower," being able to read my sister's mind or knowing when she is sad, hurt, or in trouble. But looked at differently, I know there are serious communication difficulties for twins who are learning to relate to non-twins who do not and cannot share the very intense closeness that twins share. And, obviously, non-twins have trouble when they try to understand twins’ verbal and non-verbal communication.

For example, onlookers wonder when they watch twins communicate thoughts and feelings without words: “What is your sister or brother telling you non-verbally?” These communication problems are psychologically compensated for or tolerated because of the remarkable enjoyment of being a twin, having regular companionship, and being able to understand each other without talking. Unfortunately, interdependency, over-identification, and confusion, which are aspects of twin identity, come out or can be observed as twins set up their own communication styles and try to relate to the non-twin world in general. Twin communication is a subject worthy of much further investigation.

Psychological Issues Particular to Twins

1. Too Much Sharing Is Inevitable

Twins have different psychological issues to deal with than single children. Twins have to share their parents’ attention and personal space. Having to share with your sister or brother will limit and complicate their (the twins’) singular identities and focus even more attention on their already highly noticeable twinship.

As well, children who are twins have deeply profound and intense relationships with each other, which easily causes identity confusion. One example might be personally taking on your brother's or sister's poor grade in math as if it were your grade and your fault that he or she did extremely poorly. Another example involves thinking that you can share your friends and, when you are grown-up adults, your children, because you are “copies” of one another. This assumption is clearly not true and is a wrong direction to take. Learning not to automatically share is a personal value that twins need to learn and respect. Being that I am an identical twin, I had problems because I felt guilty when I did not want to share with my family members and very close friends.

2. What Is Mine Is Not Necessarily Yours

"Who owns what" is a lesson that twins need to learn in order to develop their individuality and to deal with their confusing twin problems. With twins, everyone close tends to get involved.

Another aspect of having to learn to stop sharing is related to feeling like you are betraying your twin if you get something she/he wants to have. Giving away or showing too much interest in which twin has a special toy, dress, or pair of boots limits the twins’ ability to make their own decisions that are based on their own interests, not their twin's. A glaring example that lasted for many years was my lack of interest in exotic places and my sister’s obsession with travel. Thankfully, we never agreed on the best vacation or holiday destination, but it could have happened easily if my financial situation were stronger.

While “who makes the decisions” or “who is right or wrong” can cause enormous rage no matter how carefully twins try to be reasonable with each other, settling these ownership issues and determining who is right and who is not can be an ongoing, almost impossible challenge. My perceptions and opinions are based on my twin consulting experiences, my writing, and my own life experiences. If you are not a twin, this may be difficult to feel and fully comprehend.

Conclusions

There are distinct changes in the twin relationship as twins separate and slowly find how they are the same but also very different. If you are a twin or close to a twin, remember to value who you are as an individual and how being a twin can provide special advantages when empathy is necessary and extremely valuable. Keeping this in mind will help you get along with your twin. Sometimes you can't understand why your twin is making decisions that seem ridiculous or are sure to be ineffective. Don't bombard your twin with your opinion. Trying to understand how you see situations differently will help both of you, and any third person who is involved, to survive the argument. Remember that your opinion is just your opinion and that you are two people who see the world differently, which is healthy and seriously important to the growth of individuality.

While being a twin is fun and affords a lot of special attention, separating from your twin takes many long and hard years.

Ideas to Reflect Upon as You Develop Individuality

  1. How am I different from my twin?
  2. Why is winning so important to me?
  3. Is cutting off my relationship with my twin necessary?
  4. Can I find other twins to share my misunderstandings and disappointments with?
  5. Do my twin and I have different objects and friends that are not shared?

item.title: Consider This the Next Time You Feel the Urge to Retreat
item.description:
Meditation

Consider This the Next Time You Feel the Urge to Retreat

Four challenges we all face when we want to go to a remote place to find silence.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • We all need silence, yet what silence is varies across needs and contexts.
  • We tend to idealize how we will feel in quiet places. It's important to mind our expectations.
  • Retreating into remote locations can promote well-being, but only if we prepare for the challenges.

The fjord's crystalline water jiggles in the gentle breeze of these small hours, when I commit to writing. The glittery dew on the grass and the autumn leaves of the pear tree dance on my eyelids as I look tenderly through our cabin’s window. The birdsong does not interrupt, but if something does, it deepens my quiet.

Think of a place you have experienced as silent. What did that place look like? How did it feel to be there? Was it a solo experience, or, if not, who kept you company? Most importantly, how would you describe that sense of quiet?

There was certainly an outer and an inner soundscape, coexisting with the silent space you visited. For some, the experience might have felt idyllic. For others, such quietness, which we tend to idealize, wasn’t even pleasant, especially if that “silence” redirected your attention to the inner turmoil of your mind spinning around, despite the stillness of the surroundings.

The human search for silence has been exponentialized in the media. National Geographic [1] describes it as a luxury, and a recent report by BookRetreats [2] suggests that faraway islands' coordinates lead us to associate quiet with remoteness. Yet, the more popular our quest for quiet becomes, the more we can idealize the feelings we expect to embrace in a quiet place.

In our pilot study, Professor Brady Wagoner and I have explored various forms of silence as socially constructed experiences, rather than merely sensorial [3]. Our findings suggest that our needs in specific contexts, as much as geographical spaces, shape what we describe as quiet, and how we feel when we're there.

The Need for Silence Is Real

In popular culture, silence is often defined as what we experience in opposition to noise. By this definition, it is no wonder so many people living in cities exposed to excessive noise daydream about a holiday in remote locations. The World Health Organization[4] highlights, based on a large body of research, that noise pollution can damage our sleep and, in turn, affect the body's ability to rest and restore itself, as well as the functioning of our vital organs.

In addition, when we are exposed to excessive noise in our daily lives, WHO notes that our concentration and memory can be hindered [5]. Imagine trying to finish a school or work task or returning home already exhausted from work and not being able to relax because traffic noise outside the window keeps interrupting you. Many people would find that distressing and feel irritated. If that builds up over time, chronic stress can also cloud our health and wellbeing long-term.

The Human Search for Silence

Beyond chronic noise exposure, people have plenty of other reasons to search for quiet in their lives. I say it often: Silence has a few superpowers; two of them are enhancing attention and helping us strive for balance [6]. In my work as a researcher, clinician, and educator, I have found that people often search for pockets of silence to give themselves time and space to focus [7]. This can be, for instance, a creative project such as a book or an art piece, or an emotional room to find meaning after an illness, a heartbreak, or a career change [8].

Both in my private life and as a scholar, I have found quiet traveling to be a gift. Whether it's silent retreats, a holiday, or a family visit, there is solace in being close to nature that has soothed even the wildest sorrows. Still, at least four challenges stand in the way of most of us when we retreat from our everyday life contexts.

The first is how close one is to nature, and how far one’s routine surroundings are from that distance. For me, it is enough to lie in a hammock in my parents’ garden, looking at the Puracé Vulcan, or sit by the fireplace reading in our wooden cabin, with a glass of wine and orange-peel chocolate next to me. For some friends, it means sleeping in a tent in minus temperatures and having canned food for breakfast on the edge of a mountain peak.

The second challenge is how often we can afford to be in remote locations, in terms of time and economic resources. Some have the luxury of a place in the woods or by an archipelago within a short drive or ferry ride. Others have to pay a few thousand dollars to rent a place and must even fly to get there. The silence that remote locations offer is, then, a privilege.

The third challenge is the honest conversation we are set to have with ourselves about what motivates our urge to retreat. Distraction and avoidance are unlikely to give you the same outcome as a genuine pursuit of distance to align with your values and discern what it is that you need the most. This is closely connected with the fourth challenge.

What Kind of Silence Are You Looking For?

The fourth challenge is what happens once we can afford to be in a remote location. We are not passive recipients of whatever a geographic location offers. We actively co-create what a silent place is for us. Part of my work has been to demystify silence, so here is a spoiler alert: I don't know of a purely silent place. Not even when my students and I visited an anechoic chamber at NTNU did we find pure quiet—we heard bodily sensations that appear unimaginable to us [9].

On the one hand, there are factual markers such as low decibel levels, disconnection from the internet, and no use of electronic devices, as well as the location's architecture and natural surroundings, factors that certainly count. On the other hand, you could be in a remote cabin close to a fjord with a stunning view through your window and still feel miserable because your mind keeps spinning, or because you are constantly distracted by your phone, taking pictures or attending to notifications from social media.

As I address in my work, the best silences for our well-being are those "sweet spots" between external and internal stimuli, which help us to find balance between doing and being [10]. As a therapist, and also a person who has practiced, and thus also struggled with, meditation, it is also fair to say that going from zero to a hundred in terms of exposure to silence can be hard for the mind. We are to be gentle as we dive into the craftsmanship of silence.

While many of us might start by asking where silence is to be found, and how to get there, I challenge you to first gain clarity on what kind of silence you are longing for. Retreating, says Spanish author Pablo D’Ors [11], is meaningful only if you go inward, not merely remote.
